title: Newton's law of gravitation and field strength
source: Questions copied unchanged from the mission-lesson scripts for CCEA A-level Physics (status of the source: mission-lesson scripts of Oct-Nov 2026 (reviewed by AI reviewers; not signed off by a person)). Terms and clues: C03-uk1#t3 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t1 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t4 term and clue written for the game; C03-1#t2 term and clue written for the game. Questions: C03-1#N.3, C03-uk1#N.3, C03-1#N.8a, C03-uk1#N.8, C03-uk1#N.9a.

assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Vector
items.clue: Quantity that has both a size and a direction.

items.label: Gravitational field strength
items.clue: Force per unit mass on a small test mass, in N kg⁻¹.

items.label: Uniform field
items.clue: Model used near the surface, where g barely changes.

items.label: Inverse-square law
items.clue: Pattern in which doubling r divides the pull by four.

questions.stem: Two objects exert gravitational forces of magnitude F on each other. The mass of each object is doubled, and the distance between their centres is tripled. What is the new magnitude of the gravitational force that each object exerts on the other?
Which statement is true for the gravitational field of a point mass but not for the electric field of a point charge?

options.text: The field strength is inversely proportional to the square of the distance from the source.
The force on any test object placed in the field is always towards the source.
The field strength is defined as force per unit of a property of a small test object.
The field lines around the source are radial straight lines.

questions.explanation: Masses only attract, so the force always points to the source. An electric force on a test charge can point away from the source if the charges have the same sign.

questions.stem: The Earth exerts a gravitational force of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N on the Moon. The mass of the Moon is about 1.2% of the mass of the Earth. Which statement about the gravitational force that the Moon exerts on the Earth is correct?

options.text: It is 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, and it pulls the Earth towards the Moon.
It is about 1.2% of 2.0 × 10²⁰ N, as the Moon has far less mass.
It is zero, as a small body cannot attract a much larger one.
It is zero, as the Moon has no air and so has no gravity.

questions.stem: Two electrons are held a short distance apart, far from all other objects. Which statement correctly describes the forces the electrons exert on each other?

options.text: They exert repulsive forces of both kinds, as their charges are alike.
Each electron repels the other electrically and attracts it gravitationally.
They exert only repulsive electric forces, having too little mass for gravity.
Their gravitational attraction exceeds their electric repulsion.

questions.stem: Two equal masses are fixed a distance d apart. Separately, a charge +Q and a charge −Q are fixed a distance d apart. Which statement about the resultant field at the midpoint of each pair is correct?

options.text: It is zero for both pairs.
It is zero for the masses; for the charges it is not zero and points towards −Q.
It is not zero for the masses; for the charges it is zero.
It is zero for the masses; for the charges it is not zero and points towards +Q.

questions.explanation: Gravity only attracts, so the two pulls at the midpoint are equal and opposite. A positive test charge there is pushed away from +Q and pulled towards −Q: both towards −Q.
